title: Maintain and support sustainable wild flower harvesting practices

lessons.title: Wild flowers and why harvesting must be sustainable
lessons.html:
South Africa's wild flower industry

South Africa has one of the richest floras in the world. The Cape Floral Kingdom, with its fynbos, is famous for proteas, pincushions (Leucospermum), conebushes (Leucadendron), restios, buchu and many bulbs. Wild-harvested fynbos is sold locally and exported as fresh flowers, dried flowers and greens, and some species are used for oils and teas.

Why sustainability matters

  • Many species grow only in small areas and some are threatened.
  • Over-harvesting can stop plants setting seed, so populations shrink.
  • Fynbos depends on fire and seed to regenerate; if seed is removed, plants may not recover after the next fire.
  • Wild flowers support pollinators such as sugarbirds, sunbirds, insects and small mammals.
  • Damaged veld lets alien invasive plants like pine, hakea and acacia spread.

Legal requirements

Picking wild flowers is controlled by provincial nature conservation laws, and in many cases a permit is required, especially for protected species. Landowners and harvesters must have the right permits and follow their conditions. Your supervisor or the provincial conservation authority (such as CapeNature in the Western Cape) can confirm what applies. Never harvest on land without the owner's permission.

Sustainable harvesting standards

Some harvesters follow a sustainable harvesting code of practice or certification scheme, which buyers increasingly ask for. These typically cover how much to pick, which stems to pick, recording, worker conditions and alien plant clearing.

Know your species

Learn to identify the species you harvest, the ones you must not touch, and the stage of flowering at which they are picked. A picture guide in the field helps. If you are unsure of a plant, do not pick it; ask your supervisor.

lessons.title: Good harvesting practice in the veld
lessons.html:
Before harvesting

  • Check that the harvesting block is approved in the harvest plan and that permits are valid.
  • Know the target species, quantity and stem specifications for the order.
  • Collect clean, sharp secateurs, buckets or bins, and PPE: gloves, hat, long sleeves, boots and sunscreen.

While harvesting

  • Pick only a portion of each plant as set by the harvest plan or code of practice, leaving enough flowers to set seed. Leave plants that are young or have few flowers.
  • Cut, do not break or pull. Use clean cuts with secateurs so the plant can regrow and is not uprooted.
  • Spread harvesting across the block instead of stripping one patch.
  • Avoid trampling seedlings and other plants. Use existing paths.
  • Do not disturb nests, bees or animals.
  • Do not harvest from recently burnt areas or rested blocks.
  • Keep cut stems in shade and in water or as instructed to keep quality.

After harvesting

  • Record block, species, number of stems or bunches, date and pickers.
  • Report any signs of over-harvesting, disease, illegal picking or alien plants.
  • Take all litter, string and waste out of the veld.

Supporting conservation

  • Help with clearing alien invasive plants when scheduled.
  • Report fires and help keep firebreaks clear.
  • Respect rest periods for blocks to recover.

Safety in the veld

Fynbos areas are often steep and rocky. Work in pairs or teams, carry water, watch for snakes and bees, and know the emergency plan. Stop work in lightning or extreme heat, and report injuries immediately.

Key points

  • Harvest only with permits and landowner permission.
  • Leave enough flowers on each plant to set seed.
  • Cut cleanly with secateurs; never pull or uproot.
  • Spread harvesting and avoid trampling.
  • Record what you pick and report problems.
